messages.body_plain:
Hi Erica, thanks for the further information. Scattered thoughts:
The design fits gmultmix, but with very few observations for some species, I think phi and p may be pretty difficult to disentangle.  Maybe less important for fitting but something to think about: N (or the superpopulation M, in gmultmix) is assumed to have some parametric distribution, but 3 spatial replicates may make it challenging to find a reasonable parameter.
Don't suggest pooling the observer counts into 1 value unless the birds seen by each observer are mutually exclusive: double-counting, etc. You could pick one observers observations, I guess.
Since primary interest seems to be p, might be worthwhile to ditch the extra hierarchical level associated with gmultmix, stack site-visits combinations, and use multinomPois.  Main conceptual difference is that abundance is no longer thought of as a sort of super-population (the birds that might have been present over the duration of the survey) and instead the number of birds that might be possible to detect during a single visit.  The information used to estimate p remains the same, but you won't have availability getting in the way of things.
If one really needed to try to figure out causes of detection variance for all of these species, BUGS/JAGS will probably at least converge even for the smallest sample size, and maybe an approach conditioning N out of the likelihood would, too. I don't really know exactly at which # of observations optimization is likely to start crashing and burning.
Cheers,

John

> Dear Eunbi Kwon,

> I like the idea of what you're trying.  pcountOpen can (often) separate local and external contributions to population growth by their different signatures in the data.  In the model you're using, gamma contributes according to what the abundance at that site was the previous day, whereas iota contributes independently of that.  They're both Poisson distributed, but the fact that one depends on the abundance at the site and the other doesn't lets the model disentangle them.

> fm2 <-  pcountOpen(~area+transect, ~area+transect+weeks, ~1, ~timep+lowtidep+hitidep, dynamics="constant", mixture = "ZIP", pm.umf, K=350)
>
> In this version, gamma works like iota does in the first model, and omega represents the local contribution, which in your case would represent probability of a shorebird staying at that site another day.  That seems to be a more sensible way to represent your dynamics (entry and departure).  It will take even longer to run, unfortunately.
>
> I see some other potential issues with your code.  You have transect as a continuous covariate on lambda and iota, meaning that as transect number within an area goes up, both initial abundance and entry rate decline.  Is that what you intended, or did you mean to have transect as a categorical predictor (factor)?  Unfortunately, these models can't work with this latter approach, because you'd lose spatial replication by trying to predict abundance individually at each transect.  You might be better off leaving transect out of the predictors, unless there is a clear meaning of its effect as a continuous predictor. Dear Eunbi,

You're right - the combination of using the original DM model and having covariates on gamma (and/or omega) make the models run very slowly.  Your idea of trying it without covariates first makes sense, and should help.  You could possibly also try reducing K a bit to improve speed, but it doesn't look like you can do much there, and you'd probably want to raise it again for your final analyses anyway.

Sometimes these models actually run faster with MCMC than maximum likelihood, but then model comparison becomes more challenging.  So you might be stuck waiting on these models for a while!

Best,

Jeff

messages.subject_clean: Integrated habitat and species occurrence dynamics models
messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked community:

I am investigating occupancy patterns of a vole species that occupies discrete habitat patches and presents a metapopulation-like dynamics. I have occupancy data on four consecutive sampling seasons of over 600 habitat patches. The problem is that the habitat patches are highly dynamic between seasons, with some of them merging and separating over time, changing dimensions, and most importantly changing from suitable habitat patches to unsuitable to suitable again in subsequent seasons.

My question is if unmarked has integrated habitat and species occurrence dynamics models that could be used to analyze my type of data.

(MacKenzie, D. I., Bailey, L. L., Hines, J. E., & Nichols, J. D. (2011). An integrated model of habitat and species occurrence dynamics. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2(6), 612-622.)

Thanks in advance for any help/guidance

Helena

Dear Helena,

Unfortunately, unmarked does not have this. Since Jim Hines is an author of that paper you mention, I am quite certain that the model is incorporated into his PRESENCE software, so I would use PRESENCE. (I am not sure whether MARK has that model, may want to check.)

As I remember, their model is a version of a multistate model. These can of course be implemented in BUGS software as well, and this then confers the usual advantages of ease of extension in virtually any direction: e.g., random effects, “integrated models” (combining data sets with different protocols), ...…

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi fellow Unmarkers,

I have a question in regards of the spatial dependence model that can be run in PRESENCE (Hines et al., 2010) for both single-season and two-species models. I would have posted this question on the online forum for Presence and Mark Programs, both something is going on with their online registration at the moment. Anyways....

I am using presence/absence data along with data for a few different covariates at different spatial scales to answer questions in regards to the occurrence of a rare species of stream fish. Four spatially replicated surveys (Sur_1, Sur_2, etc) were performed to produce our detection histories, and data for 6 occupancy covariates and 3 sampling covariates were also collected. Occupancy covariates were associated with either the site scale (depth (SD), velocity (SV), woody debris (WD), substrate), or the watershed scale (stream link magnitude and %Forest cover). Sampling covariates included:  mean velocity, mean depth, and mean substrate for each spatial replicate within the site. I constructed 4  models in PRESENCE using these data and the spatial dependence model. I also constructed 4 models with the same model design (i.e., models contained exactly the same covariates), but instead were run with the single-species, single season model (as this model assumes independence among surveys). The objective was to determine which model type (spatial dependence, or simple single season) provided a better explanation of the observed data, based on AIC ranking.

Constructed models (for both the spatial dependence and simple season models) would look something like this, using the occu formulation in R

1. (~Velocity+Depth+Substrate~SV)

2. (~Velocity+Depth+Substrate~SD)

3.  (~Velocity+Depth+Substrate~LINK)

4. (~Velocity+Depth+Substrate~LINK + Forested)

Interestingly, models constructed with just the site scale-occupancy variables did not detect spatial autocorrelation (which is what I would have suspected). The models constructed with ONLY occupancy covariates at the watershed scale; however, did detect spatial autocorrrelation (as the spatial dependence version of these models were ranked higher than their simple single season counterparts) in the detection histories. My question is: why am I seeing spatial autocorrelation in the models using only the watershed scale covariates and not in the models constructed with the site scale covariates? This is very confusing!  If anyone can help me answer this conundrum it would be much appreciated!

I have attached the data if anyone wants to take a crack at it in PRESENCE,  using the models above.

Regards,

Josh

I have a simple dynamic occupancy model where starting psi, extinction and colonisation vary by treatment vs non-treatment.

  fm<-colext(psiformula=~Trt, gammaformula=~Trt, epsilonformula = ~Trt, pformula=~1, data=my.data)

To get derived estimates of occupancy for each group I wrote a function and then bootstrapped to get 95%CIs

  psi.year<-function(fm){
    psi.hat<-plogis(c(sum(coef(fm, type='psi')),coef(fm, type='psi')[1]))
    gam.hat<-plogis(c(sum(coef(fm, type='col')),coef(fm, type='col')[1]))
    eps.hat<-plogis(c(sum(coef(fm, type='ext')),coef(fm, type='ext')[1]))
    psi.mat<-matrix(NA,9,2) #9 years of data, 2 columns - treatment and nontreatment sites
    psi.mat[1,]<-psi.hat
    for(t in 2:9){
      psi.mat[t,]<-(psi.mat[t-1,]*(1-eps.hat))+((1-psi.mat[t-1,])*gam.hat)
    }
    return(c(psi.mat)) #Had to turn it into a vector so parboot would run
  }

  pb1<-parboot(fm, statistic=psi.year, nsim=100)
  psi.yr.CI <http://psi.yr.CI><-cbind(pb1_at_t0,t(apply(pb1_at_t.star,2,quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))))

Hi Abid,

Okay, I'll bite, but this sure isn't canon (this <http://warnercnr.colostate.edu/~anderson/PDF_files/Concerns.pdf> may be a useful reference among many others): opinions my own, trade-names do not suggest endorsement by the board, or the U.S. government, etc.  I suggest quickly skimming the methods sections for a sample of papers related to your work, and see how these people performed variable selection.  My guess is that you will find the process you propose is not adopted very often or even at all.  If model selection is ultimately made using an I-T approach (and it has to be), it would probably make reviewers happier to remain consistent with the selection criteria throughout the process.  A more consistent approach for exploratory analysis would be to use the dredge function (associated with library MuMIn) or some sort of stepwise procedure (see Richard Schuster's post above).  Whether this is an objectively reasonable approach is a different question.  Maybe this is more reasonable if the occupancy state or parameter is something being used for a further analysis that is the underlying motivation for the research (e.g., 'species with this general trait tend to have larger distributions in the study area', etc.), and maybe less reasonable if the purpose is to say substantive things about what truly influences the occupancy state of a single species.  If you can break your set of covariates up into a set of meaningfully distinct hypothetical models (hypotheses being the basis for both AIC and p-values), maybe all the better if the point is inference about general influences.  One pragmatic issue with an additive significance approach is that the effect of certain covariates may only be revealed via interactions.

John

I suggest starting with simpler models (a few parameters, not 16) and then adding a parameter  at a time to find out exactly which additional parameter is causing the failure.

16 parameters Is a lot, so unless you have an enormous data set it may not be possible to fit such a model.  In any case, stepwise building up of the model and using the estimates of each previous model as starting values will often solve the problem.

The order of the starting values will be exactly the order that the parameters are printed, which you can diagnose by running a simpler occupancy model and inspecting the output.

regards
andy

Hi Mark, I'm pasting the source code used to generate the summary for a parboot object below.  It should be pretty straightforward to combine the matrices of t.star fit values across the separate runs and calculate the necessary statistics using this:

    t.star <- obj...@t.star
    t0 <- object@t0
    nsim <- nrow(t.star)
    biasMat <- pMat <- matrix(NA, nsim, length(t0))
    for(i in 1:nsim) {
        biasMat[i,] <- t0 - t.star[i,]
        pMat[i,] <- abs(t.star[i,] - 1) > abs(t0 - 1)
        }
    bias <- colMeans(biasMat)
    bias.se <http://bias.se> <- apply(biasMat, 2, sd)
    p.val <- colSums(pMat) / (1 + nsim)
    stats <- data.frame("t0" = t0, "mean(t0 - t_B)" = bias,
        "StdDev(t0 - t_B)" = bias.se <http://bias.se>, "Pr(t_B > t0)" = p.val,
        check.names = FALSE)

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Dan for suggesting that I combine my two t.star matrices (resulting from separate parboot runs) into a new, single t.star matrix, on which the unmarked source code (which Dan provided) can be run, to produce combined validation statistics and p-values.

Here's the code Dan helped me with. Only the first two lines, and the last one, are new; the rest is unmarked source code...

> t.star <- rbind(sims[[1]]@t.star,sims[[2]]@t.star) #sims is the name of a list containing two parboot objects
> t0 <- sims[[1]]@t0 #OR sims[[2]]@t0 because they're the same

> nsim <- nrow(t.star)
> biasMat <- pMat <- matrix(NA, nsim, length(t0))
> for(i in 1:nsim) {
>   biasMat[i,] <- t0 - t.star[i,]
>   pMat[i,] <- abs(t.star[i,] - 1) > abs(t0 - 1)
> }
> bias <- colMeans(biasMat)
> bias.se <http://bias.se> <- apply(biasMat, 2, sd)
> p.val <- colSums(pMat) / (1 + nsim)
> stats <- data.frame("t0" = t0, "mean(t0 - t_B)" = bias,
>                     "StdDev(t0 - t_B)" = bias.se <http://bias.se>, "Pr(t_B > t0)" = p.val,
>                     check.names = FALSE)

> stats #inspect combined stats

Thanks again to Dan for taking the time to help.

Mark B.
Ph.D. Candidate
University of Saskatchewan
